intro: “Never have I seen…”, “Not only did she…”, “No sooner had we arrived than…”: when a negative or restrictive expression starts the sentence, English puts the auxiliary before the subject, as in a question. It is a way of adding emphasis, typical of speeches, articles and careful writing, and very popular in exams (FCE, IELTS, TOEIC).
objectifs: Recognise the expressions that trigger inversion (never, rarely, little, not only, under no circumstances, not until, only when…).
Make the inversion with the right auxiliary, including do / does / did.
Use the two-part structures: no sooner… than, hardly… when, not only… but also.
Know when not to invert and choose the right register.

texte: In a normal sentence, the negative adverb goes near the verb: “I have never seen such a mess.” For emphasis, you can put it at the start of the sentence. Then you need question order: auxiliary + subject + verb. “Never have I seen such a mess.”
The effect is solemn, dramatic or very written. In everyday speech, you hear it in speeches, sports commentary, advertising, or in jokes when people exaggerate.
After these expressions in first position, inversion is obligatory: “Never I have seen…” is wrong.
exemples: I have never felt so proud. → Never have I felt so proud.
Neutral → emphatic.
She rarely makes mistakes. → Rarely does she make mistakes.
No auxiliary: add “does”.
We had seldom seen such enthusiasm. → Seldom had we seen such enthusiasm.
Past perfect: “had” comes first.

texte: They are negative adverbs or phrases (never, at no time, under no circumstances), adverbs of very low frequency (rarely, seldom, hardly ever), or restrictive phrases starting with “only” or “not”.

lignes: Never before had the city been so quiet.
Seldom do we receive such kind letters.
Hardly ever does he take a day off.
not at all (with know, realise, imagine, suspect)
Little did she know what was waiting for her.
At no time was the public in danger.
Under no circumstances / On no account
On no account should you sign this.
In no way is this your fault.
Nowhere else will you find such good coffee.
Not once did he say thank you.

texte: Follow the rules for questions: if there is already an auxiliary (be, have, a modal), it moves before the subject. If not, add do / does / did and use the base form of the verb.
When “be” is the main verb, “be” itself moves: “Rarely is he late.”
The negative adverb already contains the negative idea, so do not add “not”: “Never have I seen…”, not “Never haven't I seen…”.

lignes: I didn't once see her smile.
Not once did I see her smile.
I have never been so tired.
Never have I been so tired.
You should not open it in any circumstances.
Under no circumstances should you open it.
You won't find a better price anywhere.
Nowhere will you find a better price.

sections.titre: Not until, only when, only after, only by
texte: With “Not until…” and “Only + a time or method expression”, the inversion happens in the main clause, not in the clause after “until / when / after”.
So the time clause keeps normal word order: “Not until I got home did I realise I had lost my wallet.” (not “did I get home”).
“Only” directly before a subject does not cause inversion: “Only John knows the code” (nobody else knows it).
exemples: Not until the end of the film did we understand the title.
We only understood at the end.
Only when the rain stopped did we leave the shelter.
Inversion in the main clause only.
Only after three interviews was she offered the job.
Passive: “was” comes first.
Only by working together can we solve this problem.
Method: only by + -ing.

texte: “Not only… but (also)…”: invert the first part only. “Not only did she write the report, but she also presented it.”

“No sooner… than” and “Hardly / Scarcely / Barely… when” say that one thing happened immediately after another. They are almost always used with the past perfect in the first part and the past simple in the second.
Trap: “no sooner” goes with “than” (it is a comparative); “hardly / scarcely” go with “when” (sometimes “before”). Don't mix them.
exemples: Not only is the hotel cheap, but it's also right next to the beach.
Not only… but also.
No sooner had I sat down than the phone rang.
Immediately after I sat down.
Hardly had we left the house when it started to pour.
Immediately after we left.
Scarcely had the match begun when the lights went out.
scarcely: more literary.

texte: Inversion is a choice of style. In an ordinary email or conversation, the neutral version sounds more natural: “I've never seen anything like it.” Used too often, inversion sounds pompous.
It is very effective in a speech, at the end of an essay, in an official notice (“On no account should passengers leave their luggage unattended”), or for a humorous effect.
Don't confuse it with conditional inversion (Had I known…, Should you need…), studied in lesson 160, or with emphatic do / does / did (lesson 168).
exemples: Neutral: I didn't realise until later. / Emphatic: Only later did I realise.
Same meaning, different register.
On no account should passengers leave their luggage unattended.
Official notice.
Never again will I eat seven doughnuts in one go!
Humorous effect.

formule: Negative / restrictive expression first + auxiliary + subject + verb (Never have I… / Rarely does she… / Not until X did we…)
prononciation: The main stress falls on the negative expression at the start: “NEVer have I…”, “NOT ONCE did he…”. It carries the emphasis.
The inverted auxiliary is usually weak: “Never have I seen” /ˈnevə həv aɪ ˈsiːn/, “Rarely does she” /ˈreəli dəz ʃi/.
No comma and no pause after the expression: it forms one block with the auxiliary and the subject.
erreurs: Never I have seen such a mess.
Never have I seen such a mess.
After “never” at the start: auxiliary + subject.
Rarely he goes out.
Rarely does he go out.
With no auxiliary, add does and use the base form.
Not only she speaks Arabic, but she also speaks Wolof.
Not only does she speak Arabic, but she also speaks Wolof.
Invert the first part.
No sooner had I arrived when the show began.
No sooner had I arrived than the show began.
no sooner… than; hardly… when.
Not until I got home I realised.
Not until I got home did I realise.
Invert the main clause.
Only when did the manager arrive, we started.
Only when the manager arrived did we start.
The time clause keeps normal order; the main clause is inverted.
Little he knew about the plan.
Little did he know about the plan.
“Little” first (negative meaning): inversion with did.

dialogue.contexte: In Douala, at a farewell party, Mrs Mbarga, a director who is retiring, gives a speech. Afterwards, two employees, Serge and Laure, talk about it.
lignes: When I joined this company in 1992, little did I know that I would stay for thirty years.
Little did I know = I had no idea.
Not only have you been wonderful colleagues, but you have also become my second family.
Never have I worked with people so generous. Thank you, all of you.
What a speech! Hardly had she started when people began to cry.
I know. Only when she mentioned the 1998 floods did I realise how much she had done for us.
Inversion in the main clause only.
She never complained, did she? Not once did I hear her raise her voice.
True. Seldom do you find a boss like that.
And under no circumstances will I let the new director change her coffee machine!
Humorous use of a formal structure.

mots: We seldom go to the cinema these days.
Rarely have I tasted such good food.
Scarcely had we arrived when it began to snow.
Under no circumstances should you share your password.
the facts or conditions of a situation
On no account must you open this door.
Only later did I realise my mistake.
No sooner had he left than she called.
Inversion adds emphasis to a sentence.
Inversion is typical of formal writing.
serious and correct in style, used in official situations

items: Never (I have / have I) eaten such spicy food.
have I
Rarely (does she / she does) arrive late.
does she
Not until I saw the photos (I understood / did I understand).
did I understand
Only John (knows / does John know) the password.
knows (“only” + subject: no inversion)

exercices.consigne: Complete with the auxiliary + subject + the verb in brackets.
items: Rarely ___ (she / complain) about her job.
does she complain
Never ___ (I / see) such a beautiful sunset.
have I seen
Under no circumstances ___ (you / should / open) this door.
should you open
Not until the next morning ___ (we / discover) the truth.
did we discover
No sooner ___ (he / leave) than it started to rain.
had he left
Only by working together ___ (we / can / solve) this problem.
can we solve

exercices.consigne: Rewrite the sentence starting with the word or phrase in brackets.
items: I have never been so embarrassed. (Never)
Never have I been so embarrassed.
He had no idea that he was being followed. (Little)
Little did he know that he was being followed.
We had just started the meeting when the power went off. (Hardly)
Hardly had we started the meeting when the power went off.
She wrote the report and she also presented it. (Not only)
Not only did she write the report, but she also presented it.
You must not leave your bag unattended in any circumstances. (Under no circumstances)
Under no circumstances must (should) you leave your bag unattended.

exercices.consigne: Each sentence has one mistake. Write it correctly.
items: Rarely he goes to the cinema.
Rarely does he go to the cinema.
No sooner had we arrived when the show began.
No sooner had we arrived than the show began. (or: Hardly had we arrived when the show began.)
Not until I read the letter I understood.
Not until I read the letter did I understand.
Only when did the manager arrive, we started.
Only when the manager arrived did we start.

exercices.consigne: Rewrite each emphatic sentence in neutral, everyday English (no inversion).
items: Never have I seen so many people.
I have never seen so many people.
Hardly had he arrived when the phone rang.
He had only just arrived when the phone rang.
Only after the call did I understand.
I only understood after the call. (or: I didn't understand until after the call.)
Under no circumstances should you share your password.
You should never share your password.

exercices.consigne: Write a short speech (4–5 sentences) to thank a team, a teacher or a friend, with at least four different inversions.
items: Example answer

When I started this course, little did I imagine how much I would learn. Never have I had such a patient teacher. Not only did you explain grammar clearly, but you also gave us confidence. Only now do I realise how far we have come. Seldom does a class end with so many smiles.

a_retenir: Negative or restrictive expression at the start → auxiliary + subject (question order).
With no auxiliary, add do / does / did: Rarely does she…, Not once did he…
Not until / Only when / Only after: the inversion is in the main clause.
No sooner… than; Hardly / Scarcely… when, with the past perfect in the first part.
Formal or emphatic: use it with care; “Only John knows” has no inversion.
